top_story: Two months into the war with the United States and Israel, Iran’s internal climate has hardened into a broad security crackdown, with more than 4,000 arrests, at least 21 executions, and the continued imprisonment of Nobel laureate Narges Mohammadi despite a sharp deterioration in her health. This repression has deepened as military pressure escalated: after Trump in March threatened Iran’s power grid over Hormuz, Washington on 29 April reaffirmed a naval blockade of Iranian ports, and Tehran answered with threats of “practical” retaliation and wider regional escalation. The combined effect is tightening coercion abroad and at home, as economic pressure and oil market disruption feed official siege rhetoric that is increasingly directed against Iranian society as well as external adversaries. The clearest takeaway is that the conflict is no longer contained to deterrent signaling in the Gulf; it is reshaping Iran’s domestic political order through wartime repression with acute human costs.
